title: Test-Time Compute: Why AI Pauses to Think Before Answering
meta_description: Discover how test-time compute lets AI models reason before responding, improving accuracy without scaling parameters. Key trade-offs revealed.
summary:
Researchers just demonstrated that spending 10x more compute at inference—not training—can boost LLM accuracy on complex tasks by up to 30%. The catch: this isn’t about bigger models. It’s about giving AI the space to deliberate before committing to an answer. The finding flips the script on how we scale intelligence.

Why "One Forward Pass" Was Holding AI Back

For years, the playbook for smarter AI was simple: scale up. More parameters, more training data, more flops. This "train-time compute" approach compressed knowledge into frozen weights, then deployed models in a single forward pass—token by token, with no room for second thoughts. The problem? Every token is a commitment. If the first word veers off course, the model doubles down, leading to those eerily confident hallucinations.

In practice, this rigid pipeline treated a casual email summary and a graduate-level physics problem with the same computational budget. The result: brittle reasoning on anything beyond surface-level tasks. The solution wasn’t just more training—it was rethinking how models use compute after deployment.

Inside Test-Time Compute: Architecture & Design Choices

  • Thinking Tokens: Before generating a final response, the model produces "scratchpad" tokens—intermediate reasoning steps invisible to the user. These tokens let the model explore approaches, backtrack, and refine logic without committing to an answer prematurely.
  • Tree Search: Instead of greedy decoding, the model branches into multiple reasoning paths, using a verifier to score and prune the most promising routes. This mimics how humans weigh options before deciding.
  • Self-Consistency: The model runs the same problem multiple times at high temperature, then takes a majority vote on the final answer. This reduces variance in outputs, especially for ambiguous queries.
  • Adaptive Routing: Not all problems need deep reasoning. Easy queries bypass the full pipeline, while hard ones trigger the full compute budget. This balances speed and accuracy dynamically.
  • Verifier Models: A lightweight secondary model scores reasoning paths, acting as a "critic" to guide the primary model toward better solutions. This is key for tree search efficiency.

Test-Time Compute Results vs State-of-the-Art

  • Accuracy Gains: On math and coding benchmarks, test-time compute boosts performance by 15–30% over single-pass inference, even with the same base model weights. The improvement scales with problem difficulty.
  • Hallucination Reduction: By allowing models to "think aloud" before answering, hallucination rates drop by ~40% on factual queries, as the model can self-correct early mistakes.
  • Compute Efficiency: While test-time compute increases per-query cost, it’s far cheaper than scaling parameters. A 10x compute budget at inference can outperform a 2x larger model at train time.
  • Latency Trade-offs: Deep reasoning adds 2–10 seconds of latency per query. Adaptive routing mitigates this by reserving the full pipeline for complex tasks only.

What This Means in Practice

Under the hood, test-time compute transforms AI from a one-shot predictor to a deliberative reasoner. For users, this means fewer confidently wrong answers and more reliable outputs on tasks like multi-step math, code debugging, or nuanced analysis. For developers, it shifts the cost curve: instead of spending millions on training larger models, teams can allocate compute dynamically at inference.

The catch: this isn’t a free lunch. Overthinking simple queries can degrade performance—like a student second-guessing themselves into the wrong answer. The solution? Adaptive systems that route queries based on difficulty. Chatbots like GPT-4 already use this hybrid approach, blending fast single-pass inference for easy questions with full reasoning for hard ones.

Limitations & Open Questions

Test-time compute introduces new challenges. Latency spikes from deep reasoning can frustrate users, and the cost of generating thousands of thinking tokens adds up. There’s also the risk of "overfitting to the verifier"—where models optimize for the scoring function rather than true correctness. Finally, the economics shift from one-time training costs (capex) to per-query operational expenses (opex), requiring new pricing models for AI services.

The Road Ahead

Test-time compute is the second axis of AI scaling. Alongside bigger models, it lets us allocate intelligence where it’s needed most—without brute-force parameter growth. The next frontier? Smarter verifiers, more efficient search algorithms, and hybrid systems that blend train-time and test-time compute seamlessly. One thing is clear: the era of AI that pauses to think has only just begun.

mainEntity.name: What are thinking tokens in AI models?

acceptedAnswer.text: Thinking tokens are intermediate reasoning steps generated by an AI model before producing a final answer. They act as a "scratchpad" to explore solutions without committing to an output prematurely.

mainEntity.name: How does test-time compute improve AI accuracy?

acceptedAnswer.text: Test-time compute allows models to use more inference steps—like tree search or self-consistency—to refine answers. This reduces errors and hallucinations by letting the model deliberate before responding.

mainEntity.name: What’s the trade-off between train-time and test-time compute?

acceptedAnswer.text: Train-time compute is a fixed cost (scaling model size), while test-time compute is per-query (scaling inference steps). The latter is more flexible but adds latency and operational costs.

  • Context-Aware Pointer: The AI doesn’t just track where your cursor is; it understands what’s under it. Hover over a recipe ingredient, and it knows you’re referring to an item, not a random word. This eliminates the need for explicit prompts like "add this to my shopping list."

The demos are impressive, but questions remain. How well does the model handle ambiguous inputs—for example, a vague gesture or a mumbled command? The lab’s pedigree suggests these challenges are top of mind, but real-world testing will reveal the true robustness of the approach.

Thinking Machines Labs’ release marks a turning point in AI development—one where usability takes center stage. title: Tmux for AI Engineers: Run Agents 24/7 on a VPS (Step-by-Step Guide)
meta_description: Learn how to use Tmux to keep AI agents running for days on a VPS—even if your laptop dies. Step-by-step setup for local and remote workflows.
summary:
By the end of this guide, you’ll have a Tmux session running on a VPS—keeping your AI agents like Codex or Hermes alive for hours (or days) without needing your laptop open. No more lost progress when your battery dies or your Wi-Fi drops. Here’s how to build it.

What This Tool Lets You Build

  • Persistent AI agents—Run Codex, Hermes, or other tools for days without interruptions, even if your local machine shuts down.
  • Multi-agent workflows—Split your terminal into panes to manage multiple agents working on different tasks simultaneously—like a refactor in one pane and a new feature in another.
  • Remote development—Offload heavy workloads to a VPS, freeing up your local machine while keeping full control via SSH.

Requirements Before You Start

  • A terminal (macOS, Linux, or WSL on Windows).
  • Basic command-line familiarity—you should know how to cd, ssh, and edit files.
  • A VPS (recommended: KVM2 plan from Hostinger or similar—transcript confirms this is sufficient).
  • Tmux installed—we’ll cover this in the steps, but if you’re on macOS, brew install tmux will handle it.
  • An AI agent like Codex or Hermes (optional, but the guide assumes you’re using one).

Complete Tmux Tutorial

1. Install Tmux Locally

Open your terminal and run:

brew install tmux # macOS
sudo apt install tmux # Ubuntu/Debian

Verify the install with:

tmux -V

You should see a version number—if not, check your package manager’s output for errors.

2. Start Your First Session

Launch Tmux with a named session (replace test with your project name):

tmux new -s test

You’ll see a green status bar at the bottom—this means you’re inside a Tmux session. Anything you run here will persist even if you disconnect.

3. Split Your Terminal into Panes

While inside Tmux, press Ctrl+B, then % to split the window vertically. Use Ctrl+B + arrow keys to navigate between panes. Here’s how to launch two Codex agents side by side:

# In the left pane:
codex --yolo

# Switch to the right pane (Ctrl+B → right arrow):
codex --yolo

Now you have two agents running in parallel—one could handle a refactor while the other builds a new feature.

4. Detach and Reattach (The Magic Feature)

To leave your session running without closing it, press Ctrl+B, then D (for "detach"). Your agents will keep running in the background. To reattach later:

tmux attach -t test

This works even if you close your terminal or switch networks—your VPS keeps everything alive.

5. Set Up Tmux on a VPS

SSH into your VPS (replace user@your-vps-ip with your credentials):

ssh user@your-vps-ip

Install Tmux on the VPS (same commands as above). Then start a new session:

tmux new -s ai-agents

Launch your agent inside the session—e.g., codex --yolo. Detach with Ctrl+B D, and your agent will run for days, even if you log out.

6. Use Slash Goals for Long-Running Tasks

Inside your agent (e.g., Codex or Hermes), use the /goal command to set a multi-hour task—like /goal build a 3D game shooter end-to-end. Tmux ensures the process won’t die when your laptop does.

Troubleshooting: Errors & Fixes

  • "Tmux command not found"—You didn’t install Tmux. Run brew install tmux (macOS) or sudo apt install tmux (Linux).
  • Can’t split panes—You’re not in a Tmux session. Start one with tmux new -s session-name.
  • Agent disconnects when detaching—Ensure you’re detaching with Ctrl+B D, not closing the terminal window.
  • VPS SSH connection drops—Use tmux attach -t session-name to reconnect. If the session died, check VPS uptime with uptime.

Where to Take This Further

  • Automate agent workflows—Write a script to launch multiple agents in separate Tmux panes, each with a different /goal.
  • Deploy full-stack apps—Use your VPS to host backend services (e.g., Node.js, Python) alongside your agents.
  • Monitor sessions—List active Tmux sessions with tmux ls and kill stale ones with tmux kill-session -t session-name.
  • Customize Tmux—Edit ~/.tmux.conf to change keybindings, colors, or status bar behavior (e.g., show CPU usage).

This setup puts you ahead of 99% of developers—most still run agents locally, losing progress when their laptop sleeps. With Tmux and a VPS, your agents work for you, not the other way around.

mainEntity.name: What happens if my VPS reboots?

acceptedAnswer.text: Tmux sessions won’t persist after a VPS reboot. Use a tool like `tmux-resurrect` to save/restore sessions or set up a systemd service to auto-restart agents.

mainEntity.name: Can I use Tmux without a VPS?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes—Tmux works locally to keep sessions alive if your terminal closes. But a VPS adds 24/7 uptime and remote access, which is ideal for long-running agents.

mainEntity.name: How do I share a Tmux session with a teammate?

acceptedAnswer.text: Use `tmux attach -t session-name` on the same VPS user account. For multi-user access, set up a shared user or use `tmux -S /tmp/shared-session` and adjust permissions.
